concepts.measure: No formal index or model. Complementarity is used qualitatively, in a Heckscher–Ohlin-like sense of dissimilar trade structures: Latin America exports commodities and raw materials that China needs, and Chinese goods mostly do not compete with Latin American exports. The authors, summarising Hernández's contribution, say most Latin American countries, Brazil included, are complementary with China but Mexico is not. They also report the OECD 'mainstream view' that only Mexico's exports are significantly affected by Chinese competition because the goods traded are dissimilar (PDF 8/printed 9). The title's triad 'Complementarity, Competition, and Globalisation' is the organising frame. The authors stress that relations should not be judged only in bilateral terms (Jenkins, Gonzalez-Vicente).
concepts.q: Unlike with Brazil, or indeed most other Latin American countries, there is no complementarity between the PRC and Mexico

concepts.measure: Sectoral complementarity measured with the Balassa (1965) revealed comparative advantage (RCA) index: a country's export share in sector s divided by the world export share in s, using WITS goods and IMF trade-in-services data across eight broad sectors. Complementarity means China (source) and the destination differ in RCA. It is tested in firm–country–sector–year regressions of an M&A dummy (or deal value) on RCA_CN and RCA_dest, LAC interactions and an RCA_dest×RCA_CN interaction. Before 2015, Chinese M&A went to sectors of destination advantage and Chinese disadvantage (resource-seeking). From 2015 to 2018 it went to sectors of Chinese advantage and destination disadvantage (utilities). This is an FDI-pattern measure, not a trade complementarity index or a factor-endowment (Heckscher–Ohlin) measure.
concepts.q: A country is said to have a revealed comparative advantage in a certain sector if the RCA value exceeds unity.

concepts.measure: Not formally measured (no index); ECLAC characterises LAC-China trade as inter-industry, raw materials for manufactures, documented by the technology-level structure of exports and imports (commodities 72% of exports to China vs manufactures 91% of imports from China, 2016).

Qualitative Heckscher-Ohlin-type framing: the inter-industry nature of LAC-China trade is attributed to complementarity of existing factor endowments, particularly for South American raw-material exporters. No index or model in pp. 53-100.
concepts.q: Its inter-industry ... nature is mainly the result of the complementarity between ... their respective existing endowments of productive factors, ... particularly in the case of the South American economies that export ... raw materials.

concepts.measure: Sectoral/structural complementarity measured descriptively with GTAP 10 (2014) data on three dimensions: sectoral value added in GDP (Table 2), export tendency, i.e. exports/sectoral output (Table 3), and import dependency of domestic consumption (Table 4). It is then embedded in a Heckscher–Ohlin/comparative-advantage framing in which Chinese capital expands LAC's resource-intensive, capital-intensive, export-oriented sectors. The paper computes no formal trade-complementarity index. The author also says the 'complementarities of factors in production' explain the factor-price results.
concepts.q: China and LAC economies are complementary

gaps.gap: No formal complementarity measure (no trade complementarity or export-similarity index, no RCA). Complementarity versus competition is asserted qualitatively and largely delegated to the issue's other articles (Jenkins on Brazil, Hernández on Mexico, Gonzalez-Vicente on Peru, Gachúz on Chile, Hearn on Cuba).

Trade, FDI and aid figures are region- or hemisphere-wide aggregates. No country-level trade or FDI values except Brazil's total trade with China (>56 bn USD, 2010) and Venezuela's ~20% oil export share. Brazil, Argentina and Peru are named as main FDI recipients without amounts.
No commodity-level trade composition (shares of copper, iron ore, soy or oil in exports to China) and no import-side data on Chinese manufactures.
Nothing on lithium, other critical minerals, refining/processing capacity, batteries, EVs, electronics or other high-tech value chains. Value-chain discussion stops at extraction and exports.

FDI measurement problem flagged by the authors: ECLAC figures exclude flows routed through tax havens. PRC official data (22 bn USD cumulative to 2006) fall to about 1.9 bn USD without tax havens. Greenfield vs. M&A is not distinguished.
Finance figures mix measure types: Venezuela loans are 'announced' (>32 bn USD), the IDB 350 m USD is 'committed', and aid/investment 2002–07 is 'combined values'. No disbursement data.
Firms and partners in the Chilean copper JV (2005, 2 bn USD) and in the 2011 Xi-tour agreements are not named. Contents and values of those agreements are not given.
Data end in 2010–2011. The document predates the post-2012 commodity downturn and later Chinese lending, investment and critical-minerals activity.
Factual error to flag: the text calls Chile 'A member of NAFTA' (PDF 14/printed 15), which it is not.
No discussion of Chinese technology, capital-goods or labour endowments beyond general state-capacity remarks. Brazil–China S&T cooperation is mentioned without any projects.
No country-level regression results. LAC is a pooled dummy, and RCA is computed for LAC as a region (Table 2), not per country.

Sectors are eight broad aggregates. 'Basic Materials & Energy' merges mining, metals, oil and gas; 'Health and Technology' merges pharma and tech. Lithium, copper, iron ore, rare earths and batteries cannot be separated, and processing/refining stages are not identified.

M&A only (Thomson Reuters, 2001–2018). Greenfield FDI, policy-bank loans, EPC contracts and offtake agreements are excluded, which understates Chinese presence in Venezuela, Argentina, Ecuador and Peru (p. 8).
Data end in 2018. Post-2018 trends (energy-transition minerals, COVID-era deals, 2020s lithium investments) are not covered. The 2020 counter-cyclical FDI claim has no LAC-specific data.

The 'complementarity' measure is export-based RCA (trade performance), not a measure of factor endowments such as reserves, land, labour or capital. Reserves, production volumes and processing capacity are absent.
Figures 2–6, 8 and 11 have no extractable values in the text. Only Tables 1, 2 and A.1–A.6 give numbers.
Country-specific deal evidence is limited to Brazil (aggregate M&A totals) and two 2019 Chile and Peru electricity acquisitions. No named mining or energy-resource deals are given.
Excess-capacity proxies (three-year fixed-asset investment, PPI) are measured at Chinese sector level. Capacity utilisation by sector is only available from 2016.
There are internal inconsistencies (p. 15 text versus Table A.1 signs; fn 12 table reference; PPI sign) that need replication or the published version.
Pages 1-52 contain no LAC-specific Chinese FDI data (by country/sector, announced vs realised); chapter IV's LAC section starts on PDF p. 53 (other analyst).
Lithium is not mentioned anywhere in the document; nickel, cobalt and rare earths are also absent from pp. 1-52.

Copper, iron ore, silver, lead, zinc and oil exports are given only as LAC aggregates (Table III.1); no country of origin (e.g. Chile/Peru for copper) and no data on processing capacity or ownership of mines.
Loan data are commitments (estimates from an unpublished Gallagher-Cipoletta paper), not disbursements; the US$74 bn loan-for-oil figure's four-year window is undated.
Swap values on Map I.2 cannot be reliably attributed to individual countries from the extracted text.
Country-level values in Figures III.8-III.9 (exporting firms and products per firm) are not reliably recoverable from the text.

Technology/STI comparisons (R&D, patents, fourth industrial revolution) are in chapter VI (PDF p. 80+), outside this range; within pp. 1-52 the capability gap is evidenced only by trade technology content and education indicators.
Data end in 2016 (2017 are projections).

No lithium, copper, nickel/cobalt or rare-earth data in PDF 53-100: no reserves, production shares, processing/refining or battery value chains. Minerals appear only as aggregate 'mining'/'metals' shares of Chinese FDI plus two named deals (CMOC niobium/phosphates in Brazil; Shandong Gold Veladero in Argentina).
No country breakdown of Chinese FDI by sector. Country totals (Figure IV.11) mix M&A values and announced projects, not realised FDI, and end in October 2017.
Chinese renewable-energy investment and Chinese bank loans are not broken down by sector within each country.
Turnkey contract data give country shares only; no named projects, and signed vs executed measures differ.
No data on Chinese technology/digital FDI (e.g. telecom firms) by country or firm, despite the telecom sector being named as a growing target.
STI comparisons are China vs LAC capability gaps; no data on actual China-LAC technology cooperation or transfer.
No US comparison for LAC finance or infrastructure (comparison is with IDB, World Bank, CAF).
Food complementarity is asserted in the concluding remarks without data in this part (trade data are in Part A).

Simulation tables (Tables 5–12) and the sectoral ODI chart (Fig. 2) are images; full country-by-sector capital-stock shocks, output, export and factor-price changes are not available in the text. Only ranges and selected values in the prose can be used.

21-sector GTAP aggregation: 'Mining' lumps coal, crude oil, gas and all minerals, so lithium, copper, iron ore, nickel and so on cannot be separated, and there is no processing/refining stage. 'Mineral products' combines ferrous and non-ferrous metals and metal products.
No critical-minerals or battery value-chain analysis; lithium appears once (p.14/247) and is not quantified.
Benchmark economy is 2014 (GTAP 10), while the ODI stock runs to 2019; there are no post-2019 data (e.g. EV, battery or lithium investments of 2020–2023).

ODI values come from project databases (RED ALC–China, CGIT). The text does not say whether they are announced or realised, whether they include construction contracts, or how greenfield and M&A are split. No firm names or individual transactions are reported (appendix 'available upon request').
Panama's sectoral ODI shares are not reported in the prose; Nicaragua and other countries are only in 'rest of LAC'.

Model assumes full employment and perfect competition, with no repatriation of profits or foreign-ownership income described, so employment effects, GNP/welfare effects and the distribution of rents between Chinese owners and host economies cannot be inferred.
No technology-transfer, human-capital or R&D variables in the model; the technology-absorption arguments are proposals only.
Some reported figures are internally inconsistent (US GDP 0.12–0.98% vs 0.12–0.18%; rest of LAC 0.77% vs 1%; Chile's export value 161,074.4; Argentina's EGW share identical to Peru's).
